entries.eli5: Takes raw text and repeatedly merges the most frequent pairs of characters into new tokens, building a vocabulary that can represent any text efficiently - like creating compound words from letters.
entries.purpose: Convert variable-length text into a fixed-vocabulary sequence of integer token IDs with full coverage of arbitrary Unicode text via byte-level fallback.
entries.input_dataset: Large raw text corpus (ideally domain-matched to the target model's training data).
usecase_scenarios: Building the subword vocabulary for a new foundation model
Handling rare words, code, and multilingual text via byte-level fallback
Controlling sequence length / efficiency trade-off via merge rules
entries.outcome: A trained tokenizer (vocab + merge rules) that encodes text to IDs and decodes IDs back to text losslessly.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N log V) encoding; O(C * M) training merges over corpus of size C
pros: Optimal merge count balances vocab size vs. sequence length
Battle-tested in GPT-2/3/4, Llama, Claude-family models
cons: Training merge greedy and can be suboptimal
No explicit semantic notion in tokens
Vocabulary artifacts across languages can be skewed
metadata.implementation_guide: Train on 10-20GB of high-quality, deduplicated text using the HuggingFace tokenizers library (Rust backend) for speed. Set vocab_size to 100k-150k. Reserve the first 4-10 IDs for special tokens (pad, eos, bos, unk, and chat-template markers) which are mandatory for chat formatting.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses a custom BPE tokenizer with ~100k vocab, optimized for code and multilingual coverage. Special tokens mark tool calls and human/assistant turns.
references: Sennrich et al. 2016 'Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units'
metadata.code_snippet:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import BPE
from tokenizers.trainers import BpeTrainer
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import ByteLevel

tok = Tokenizer(BPE(unk_token='<unk>'))
tok.pre_tokenizer = ByteLevel(add_prefix_space=False)
trainer = BpeTrainer(vocab_size=100000,
    special_tokens=['<pad>','<eos>','<bos>','<unk>'])
tok.train(files=['corpus.txt'], trainer=trainer)
enc = tok.encode('Hello, world!')
print(enc.ids)  # list of int IDs

entries.eli5: Instead of greedily merging pairs, it treats tokenization as a probabilistic puzzle: it finds the statistically most likely way to cut a sentence into pieces, which makes it great for languages without clear spaces like Japanese.
entries.purpose: Provide language-agnostic subword segmentation via Unigram LM (probabilistic segmentation) or BPE, trained directly on raw text without pre-splitting by spaces.
entries.input_dataset: Raw multilingual corpus; no whitespace pretokenization required.
usecase_scenarios: Multilingual models (LLaMA, Gemma, T5, Claude use SP-style tokenizers)
Languages without explicit word boundaries (CJK, Thai)
entries.outcome: A probabilistic subword model with piece scores; encoding uses Viterbi search for the most likely segmentation.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N * K) Viterbi segmentation where K = candidate pieces per position
pros: Trains on raw text directly (no pretokenizer bias)
Unigram model offers multiple segmentations (useful for sampling/augmentation)
cons: Slightly slower than pure BPE at inference
Probabilistic segmentation adds nondeterminism unless configured otherwise
Character coverage hyperparameter needs tuning per language mix
metadata.implementation_guide: Use the sentencepiece Python/C++ API. For highly multilingual models, set character_coverage=1.0 to ensure all CJK/Arabic characters are covered. Use model_type=unigram for better handling of agglutinative languages. Export the model to a .model file and load it via HuggingFace for seamless integration.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's tokenizer handles many languages and code formats with high efficiency. SentencePiece-style training ensures rare scripts and code identifiers are well-covered.
references: Kudo & Richardson 2018 'SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer'
metadata.code_snippet:
import sentencepiece as spm

spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    input='corpus.txt',
    model_prefix='m',
    vocab_size=100000,
    model_type='unigram',
    character_coverage=1.0,
    split_by_whitespace=False,
    normalization_rule_name='nmt_nfkc')
sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='m.model')
ids = sp.encode('Hello, world!')

entries.eli5: OpenAI's super-fast BPE implementation used by GPT-3.5/4 - written in Rust, with a regex-based pre-tokenizer that splits text into words/numbers/punctuation before BPE merges happen.
entries.purpose: Provide a high-throughput byte-level BPE with a fixed regex pre-tokenization pattern that ensures consistent behavior across Unicode text, code, and numbers.
entries.input_dataset: Trained BPE vocab + merge ranks; pattern is hand-designed, not learned.
usecase_scenarios: Fast token counting for cost estimation
entries.outcome: A 100k-200k vocab BPE with O(1) merge lookup per token; encoding throughput >100 MB/s.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N * avg_merges_per_token) encoding
cons: Fixed pattern may not be optimal for non-Latin scripts
Closed vocab training (ranks are released, not the training script)
metadata.implementation_guide: Use the tiktoken Python package. For GPT-4o use the o200k_base encoding. To build your own tiktoken-compatible tokenizer, train a BPE on byte-level tokens and export the merge ranks. The cl100k regex pattern splits text into: contractions, words, numbers (1-3 digit chunks), and whitespace.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses its own BPE variant, not tiktoken, but follows similar principles. Token counts for API billing are computed via the model-specific tokenizer.

entries.algorithm_name: Data Curation Pipeline (Dedup, Filter, Quality Score)
entries.eli5: The garbage-in-garbage-out fix: web text is full of duplicates, boilerplate, and junk - so before training, deduplicate, filter out junk, and keep the cream, because data quality beats data quantity.
entries.purpose: Construct pretraining corpora via exact/near dedup (MinHash LSH), heuristic filters, and quality classifiers to maximize benchmark-relevant knowledge per token.
entries.input_dataset: Raw web crawls (Common Crawl), books, code, papers.
usecase_scenarios: Pretraining corpus construction (the secret sauce of LLM quality)
entries.outcome: High-quality, deduplicated, mixture-weighted corpus - the dominant factor in final model quality.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N) MinHash for N documents; O(N log N) clustering
pros: Removing junk reduces memorization and benchmark contamination
cons: Pipeline engineering heavy (Spark/cluster jobs)
Over-filtering can harm long-tail knowledge and multilingual coverage
metadata.implementation_guide: Use Apache Spark or Ray for distributed processing. Step 1: Exact dedup via MD5/SHA hashes. Step 2: Fuzzy dedup via MinHash LSH (Jaccard threshold ~0.8). Step 3: Heuristic filters (remove docs with >30% URLs, too short, high perplexity under a small n-gram model). Step 4: Train a fastText classifier on high-quality seed data (Wikipedia, Books) to score and filter the rest.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Anthropic has stated that data quality and curation are critical to Claude's helpfulness and honesty. They use a multi-stage filtering pipeline with both heuristic and model-based quality scoring. Constitutional AI principles are also embedded in the data selection criteria.
references: Penedo et al. 2023 'The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM'
Lee et al. 2022 'Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better'

entries.eli5: Don't dump every kind of text in at once - mix the recipe (50% web, 20% code, 10% math, 5% books) and sometimes teach easier stuff first, then harder, like a school syllabus.
entries.purpose: Determine optimal sampling weights across domains (web/code/math/multilingual) and optionally order examples by difficulty to maximize capability per compute.
entries.input_dataset: Curated multi-domain corpus with domain labels.
usecase_scenarios: Pretraining mixture tuning (Llama-3, DeepSeek, Phi recipes)
Late-stage math/code up-sampling for reasoning models
Curriculum for stable training of small models
entries.outcome: A weighted sampler that over-samples high-value domains (code, math) and under-samples redundant web data, often with temperature-controlled mixing: p_i proportional to n_i^temperature.
benchmark_metrics: Downstream benchmark gains per domain token

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N) sampling; negligible overhead
pros: Free capability gains (10-30% on coding/math benchmarks at equal FLOPs)
cons: Optimal mixture is empirical and architecture-dependent
Aggressive up-sampling causes overfitting on small domains
metadata.implementation_guide: Use DoReMi or gradient-based mixture optimization to find optimal weights. A common recipe (Llama-3-style): ~50% web text, ~25% code, ~10% math, ~10% books, ~5% multilingual. Apply sampling temperature: p_i = n_i^0.3 / sum(n_j^0.3). For curriculum, train first 80% on general mix, then 20% on a math/code-heavy mix to boost reasoning.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's pretraining heavily weights code and math to support its strong reasoning capabilities. The mixture is dynamically adjusted during training, with a higher-quality reasoning-focused mix in the final phase.

entries.eli5: Use an existing smart LLM to write fresh, high-quality training material - like a teacher writing new problem sets - so the new model learns from curated textbook content instead of noisy web text.
entries.purpose: Generate large volumes of high-quality, instruction-rich, or domain-specific synthetic data (math problems, code, reasoning traces) to augment pretraining or SFT.
entries.input_dataset: Seed prompts + a strong teacher LLM (e.g., GPT-4, Claude) + filtering criteria.
usecase_scenarios: Phi-style textbook quality pretraining (Microsoft Phi series)
entries.outcome: Filtered synthetic datasets that boost capability beyond what web data alone provides; especially powerful for math/reasoning.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N_gen) teacher inference + O(N_gen) filtering
pros: Solves cold-start for new domains (math, rare languages)
Enables reasoning-model distillation (R1 to smaller models)
cons: Teacher biases and hallucinations propagate
Mode collapse without careful prompting/diversity filters
Licensing/attribution concerns if using proprietary teachers
metadata.implementation_guide: Use a 3-stage pipeline: 1) Generate diverse seeds (topics, difficulty, format) using a teacher LLM with high temperature (0.9). 2) Generate the actual data with structured prompts. 3) Filter rigorously - use a strong LLM as judge, dedup via MinHash, and reject outputs that do not pass unit tests (for code) or answer checks (for math). Phi-3 used ~3.3T tokens of heavily filtered synthetic data.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Anthropic uses synthetic data for both SFT and Constitutional AI revisions. The teacher is typically a stronger Claude checkpoint, and the synthetic data is filtered through constitutional principles to ensure safety and helpfulness.
references: Gunasekar et al. 2023 'Textbooks Are All You Need' (Phi-1)
metadata.code_snippet:
import anthropic, re
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
def gen_math(topic, difficulty):
    r = client.messages.create(model='claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022',
        max_tokens=1024, messages=[{'role':'user',
        'content': f'Generate one {difficulty} math problem about {topic}. Format: Problem: ...\nAnswer: <num>'}])
    return r.content[0].text
def filter_ok(t):
    return bool(re.search(r'Answer:\s*\d+', t))
raw = [gen_math('algebra','hard') for _ in range(10000)]
clean = [t for t in raw if filter_ok(t)]

entries.eli5: Make sure the model has not accidentally seen the test answers before the exam - scan training data for any overlap with benchmark questions and remove them.
entries.purpose: Detect and remove overlap between training data and evaluation benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, etc.) to get trustworthy capability measurements.
entries.input_dataset: Training corpus + benchmark question/answer strings.
usecase_scenarios: Canary-string based contamination tracking (insert canaries into private data)
entries.outcome: Clean eval scores that reflect true generalization rather than memorization; reproducible leaderboards.
benchmark_metrics: Delta between contaminated and decontaminated scores

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N_benchmarks * N_corpus * n) for n-gram search; indexable
pros: Canary strings enable detection of unauthorized training on private data
cons: Fuzzy contamination (paraphrased) is hard to detect
Removing all near-matches may over-prune legitimate knowledge
metadata.implementation_guide: Use a 13-gram Bloom filter approach: hash all 13-grams from benchmark questions into a Bloom filter, then stream the corpus and flag any document containing a match. For private data, inject unique canary strings (e.g., CANARY-uuid) and check downstream models' ability to recite them - if a model can, your data was used.
dependencies: Bloom filter or suffix array index
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Anthropic publicly commits to contamination-free evaluation of Claude. Their eval suite includes both public benchmarks (with contamination filtering) and private held-out sets that are never seen during training.
references: Carlini et al. 'Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models'
Brown et al. 2024 'Pre-training Data Leakages and Contamination'

entries.eli5: Special turn markers (like IM_START for the start of a message) tell the model who is speaking and where one turn ends - the punctuation that turns a base text model into a chatbot.
entries.purpose: Define a deterministic serialization format for multi-turn conversations, tool calls, system prompts, and (in reasoning models) thinking traces - using reserved special tokens.
entries.input_dataset: Conversation data with role labels (system/user/assistant/tool).
usecase_scenarios: ChatML (OpenAI), Llama-3 format, Claude format, DeepSeek format
Reasoning trace formatting (R1/o1 style thinking tags)
entries.outcome: A lossless text-to-conversation parser; loss masking only computes loss on assistant tokens.
benchmark_metrics: Loss-mask coverage (only assistant tokens trained on)

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L) string formatting
pros: Decouples data format from model code
Jinja templates are declarative and version-controllable
cons: Template bugs cause silent training data corruption
Special tokens must be added to tokenizer AND embedding matrix
metadata.implementation_guide: Use HuggingFace chat_template with Jinja2. Define special tokens: IM_START, IM_END (or [INST], [/INST] for Llama). The template wraps each message: '<im_start>{role}\n{content}<im_end>'. For loss masking, compute labels where user/system tokens are -100 (ignored by cross-entropy) and only assistant tokens are trained on.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses a custom chat format with Human/Assistant turn markers, plus special tokens for tool use, citations, and (in Claude 3.5+) thinking traces. The format is enforced at training and inference time.

from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('meta-llama/Llama-3-8B-Instruct')
msgs = [{'role':'system','content':'You are helpful.'},
        {'role':'user','content':'Hi!'},
        {'role':'assistant','content':'Hello!'}]
# Render to a single string with special tokens
prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
# Tokenize with loss masking (only assistant tokens count)
input_ids = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=True, return_dict=True)

entries.eli5: Turns each token ID into a long list of numbers (a vector) that captures its meaning, and adds position information so the model knows word order.
entries.purpose: Map discrete token IDs to continuous dense vectors and inject positional information into the input representation.
entries.input_dataset: Integer token ID sequences from the tokenizer.
usecase_scenarios: First layer of every transformer LLM
Initializing vocabulary for pretrained embedding reuse or extension
entries.outcome: A sequence of d_model-dimensional vectors where semantic and positional information is entangled, ready for transformer blocks.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L * d_model) for sequence length L
pros: Tied input/output embeddings save parameters (weight tying)
cons: Fixed max positions in learned absolute embeddings limits context length
Vocab-size dependent memory: vocab_size * d_model * 2 bytes can be GBs
metadata.implementation_guide: Use torch.nn.Embedding. To save massive amounts of memory (10-20% of total params), implement weight tying by sharing the weights between the input Token Embedding matrix and the final output Language Model Head (LM Head). Set padding_idx=0 and ensure the optimizer ignores gradients for this index.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude ties input/output embeddings and uses RoPE (no learned absolute positional embedding), giving it flexible long-context behavior without retraining the embedding table.
references: Vaswani et al. 2017 'Attention Is All You Need'
Press & Wolf 2017 'Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models' (weight tying)

entries.eli5: Instead of adding position information to word vectors, it rotates pairs of numbers in the query/key vectors by an angle that depends on how far apart the words are - distance between tokens emerges naturally from rotations.
entries.purpose: Inject relative position information into attention by rotating query/key vectors with position-dependent rotation matrices; relative distances translate into relative phase shifts.
entries.input_dataset: Query/key vectors of shape [B, H, L, d_head].
usecase_scenarios: Default positional scheme in Llama, Claude, Gemma, Mistral, Qwen
Efficient long-context extension via frequency scaling (NTK, YaRN)
Reducing positional interpolation artifacts in extrapolation
entries.outcome: Attention logits that depend on relative position (m - n), with smooth extrapolation behavior.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L * d_head) extra multiply-adds; negligible vs attention
pros: Relative-position-aware attention without explicit relative matrices
Compatible with FlashAttention and KV caching
Scales gracefully with NTK/YaRN frequency interpolation
cons: Weak extrapolation beyond trained length without scaling tricks
Implementation details (interleaving vs half-split) must match training for fine-tuning compatibility
metadata.implementation_guide: Implement 2D rotation matrices. Precompute the cos/sin frequency caches up to max_seq_len and register them as buffers. Use a high theta_base (e.g., 500,000) for better long-context extrapolation. Apply the rotation to the Q and K tensors before the attention dot-product. Do not apply it to V.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses RoPE with carefully tuned base frequency and possibly YaRN-style scaling for its 200k+ token context windows. The exact theta and scaling strategy is proprietary.
references: Su et al. 2021 'RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding'
metadata.code_snippet:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, math
class RoPE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, head_dim, max_seq_len=8192, theta=500000.0):
        super().__init__()
        inv_freq = 1.0 / (theta ** (torch.arange(0, head_dim, 2).float() / head_dim))
        pos = torch.arange(max_seq_len).float()
        freqs = torch.einsum('i,j->ij', pos, inv_freq)
        self.register_buffer('cos', freqs.cos()[:, None, :])
        self.register_buffer('sin', freqs.sin()[:, None, :])
    def forward(self, x):
        # x: [B, H, L, d_head]
        x1, x2 = x[..., ::2], x[..., 1::2]
        cos, sin = self.cos[:x.size(2)], self.sin[:x.size(2)]
        return torch.stack([x1*cos - x2*sin, x1*sin + x2*cos], dim=-1).flatten(-2)

entries.eli5: Skips adding position info to the vectors entirely - it just penalizes attention scores more and more the farther apart two words are, like giving far-apart words a fine.
entries.purpose: Add a fixed, non-learned linear penalty to attention scores proportional to token distance, enabling strong length extrapolation.
entries.input_dataset: Attention logits computed from QK^T.
usecase_scenarios: Models needing zero-cost length extrapolation (MPT, BLOOM, some code models)
entries.outcome: Attention that smoothly degrades with distance and extrapolates to much longer sequences than trained on.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(H * L^2) additive bias, fused into attention kernels
pros: Excellent length extrapolation without scaling hacks
No positional embedding tables or RoPE precompute
Trivially compatible with sliding window attention
cons: Slightly worse perplexity at short lengths vs RoPE on some benchmarks
Monotonic distance penalty may underuse very long-range structure unless slopes tuned
metadata.implementation_guide: Compute the slopes for each head as 2^(-8/H * (i+1)). Create a distance matrix |i - j| and multiply it by the slopes. Add this bias matrix directly to the Q @ K^T attention logits before applying the softmax. No positional embeddings are added to the input tokens.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude does not use ALiBi (it uses RoPE), but ALiBi-style distance penalties can be combined with RoPE for extra extrapolation. Some long-context variants of open models use this hybrid.
references: Press et al. 2022 'Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation'
metadata.code_snippet:
import torch
def alibi_bias(batch, heads, seq_len, device):
    slopes = torch.tensor([2**(-(2**-(i+1))) for i in range(heads)], device=device)
    slopes = slopes * (8 / heads)  # scale
    dist = torch.arange(seq_len, device=device).unsqueeze(0) - torch.arange(seq_len, device=device).unsqueeze(1)
    bias = -dist.abs().float() * slopes[:, None, None]
    return bias.unsqueeze(0).expand(batch, -1, -1, -1)
# Add to attention logits: logits = Q@K^T / sqrt(d) + alibi_bias

entries.algorithm_name: NoPE (No Positional Encoding) for Causal Models
entries.eli5: Skip position info entirely - the model figures out word order just from the causal mask (each word only sees earlier words). Surprisingly works fine and extrapolates perfectly.
entries.purpose: Eliminate explicit positional encoding entirely; rely on the causal mask to provide implicit order information, with no position-induced length limit.
entries.input_dataset: Token embeddings (no positional augmentation).
usecase_scenarios: Decoder-only causal LMs that need infinite-length extrapolation
Theoretical studies of what attention learns without positional priors
entries.outcome: Models that extrapolate to arbitrary context lengths with no RoPE/ALiBi tuning; slightly worse at short lengths but more robust at very long lengths.

metadata.computational_complexity: Zero overhead vs positional approaches
cons: Slightly worse short-context quality vs RoPE
Only works for causal/decoder models, not bidirectional encoders
metadata.implementation_guide: Simply omit the positional encoding step. The causal mask (each token attends only to itself and prior tokens) is sufficient for the model to learn order. Useful as a baseline or for very-long-context experiments.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Not used by Claude, but worth knowing for context-extension research.
references: Kazemnejad et al. 2023 'The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers'
metadata.code_snippet:
# In a decoder-only transformer:
class Block(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        # NO positional encoding added here
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x), causal=True)
        x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))
        return x

entries.algorithm_name: LongRoPE / Dynamic NTK / Dual-Level Position Interpolation
entries.eli5: Smarter RoPE scaling that searches for the best frequency-stretching plan using evolution - lets a 4k-trained model stretch to 2M tokens with a tiny bit of fine-tuning.
entries.purpose: Extrapolate RoPE beyond trained context by searching per-frequency scaling factors (rather than uniform NTK), achieving 8x-512x context extension with minimal quality loss.
entries.input_dataset: Short-context pretrained checkpoint + small long-context fine-tune data.
usecase_scenarios: Cheap long-context adaptation of any RoPE model
entries.outcome: Models that work at 1M-2M token context with negligible quality loss in the original window, after a brief (1B token) long-context fine-tune.

metadata.computational_complexity: Zero inference cost; search is offline
pros: Much better extrapolation than uniform NTK
Per-frequency optimization avoids the locality/long-range trade-off
cons: Search adds engineering complexity
Requires long-context fine-tune data for stability
metadata.implementation_guide: Use the LongRoPE recipe: 1) Define a 2D search space of per-frequency scaling factors. 2) Use evolutionary search to maximize needle-in-haystack performance on a held-out long-context set. 3) Apply the searched factors during fine-tuning. 4) Optionally use a dual-approach: separately fine-tune a long-context version, then merge weights with the original for short-context preservation.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's 200k+ context is achieved with a combination of careful RoPE tuning, long-context fine-tuning, and (likely) some form of position interpolation. The exact recipe is proprietary.
references: Chen et al. 2024 'LongRoPE: Extending LLM Context Beyond 2 Million Tokens'
metadata.code_snippet:
# After searching optimal per-freq scales (list of floats):
class ScaledRoPE(RoPE):
    def __init__(self, head_dim, max_seq_len, theta, scales):
        inv_freq = 1.0 / (theta ** (torch.arange(0, head_dim, 2).float() / head_dim))
        inv_freq = inv_freq / scales  # per-freq scaling
        pos = torch.arange(max_seq_len).float()
        freqs = torch.einsum('i,j->ij', pos, inv_freq)
        self.register_buffer('cos', freqs.cos()[:, None, :])
        self.register_buffer('sin', freqs.sin()[:, None, :])

entries.eli5: Splits the model's understanding into many heads, each of which looks at the sentence differently - one might track grammar, another pronoun references - and then merges their views.
entries.purpose: Compute token-to-token interactions via scaled dot-product attention in parallel across H heads with different learned projections, giving the model multiple representation subspaces.
entries.input_dataset: Sequence of hidden states [B, L, d_model].
usecase_scenarios: Core building block of every transformer LLM
Baseline for comparing efficient attention variants
Cross-attention in encoder-decoder and multimodal models
entries.outcome: Contextualized representations where each token aggregates information from all others, weighted by learned relevance.
benchmark_metrics: Attention entropy and head specialization measures
FLOPs and memory vs accuracy trade-off curve

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L^2 * d_model) time, O(L^2 * H) naive attention memory (O(L) with FlashAttention)
pros: Provably expressive (can simulate Turing machines at sufficient precision)
cons: Quadratic cost in sequence length
KV cache at inference scales with heads - memory bottleneck for long context serving
metadata.implementation_guide: Implement standard Q, K, V linear projections. For the forward pass, use torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal=True to automatically apply the lower-triangular mask and utilize optimized backend kernels (Flash/MemEfficient).
metadata.claude_specific_notes: MHA is the baseline. Claude and most modern frontier models have moved to GQA or MLA for memory efficiency at long context, but MHA remains the reference architecture.
references: Vaswani et al. 2017 'Attention Is All You Need'
metadata.code_snippet:
import torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
class MHA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.d_head = d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3*d_model, bias=False)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        B,L,D = x.shape
        qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B,L,3,self.n_heads,self.d_head).permute(2,0,3,1,4)
        q,k,v = qkv[0], qkv[1], qkv[2]  # [B,H,L,d]
        # SDPA auto-uses FlashAttention
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True)
        return self.out(a.transpose(1,2).reshape(B,L,D))

In the attention forward pass, repeat the K and V tensors along the head dimension using torch.repeat_interleave to match the number of Q heads before computing the dot product.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
class GQA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, n_kv_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads, self.n_kv = n_heads, n_kv_heads
        self.d_head = d_model // n_heads
        self.q = nn.Linear(d_model, n_heads*self.d_head, bias=False)
        self.k = nn.Linear(d_model, n_kv_heads*self.d_head, bias=False)
        self.v = nn.Linear(d_model, n_kv_heads*self.d_head, bias=False)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        B,L,_ = x.shape
        q = self.q(x).reshape(B,L,self.n_heads,self.d_head).transpose(1,2)
        k = self.k(x).reshape(B,L,self.n_kv,self.d_head).transpose(1,2)
        v = self.v(x).reshape(B,L,self.n_kv,self.d_head).transpose(1,2)
        # Repeat k,v to match q heads
        rep = self.n_heads // self.n_kv
        k = k.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1); v = v.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1)
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True)
        return self.out(a.transpose(1,2).reshape(B,L,-1))

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
def sliding_window_attn(q, k, v, window=1024):
    # q,k,v: [B,H,L,d]
    B,H,L,d = q.shape
    # Build band mask: 1 where |i-j| <= window//2
    i = torch.arange(L, device=q.device)[:,None]
    j = torch.arange(L, device=q.device)[None,:]
    mask = (i - j).abs() <= window // 2
    mask = mask.tril()  # also causal
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2,-1)) / (d**0.5)
    scores = scores.masked_fill(~mask[None,None,:,:], float('-inf'))
    return F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ v

entries.eli5: Compress the KV cache into a tiny 'latent' vector per token, then decompress on the fly during attention - shrinks the cache 10-100x vs MHA while keeping quality, perfect for million-token context.
entries.purpose: Project K/V into a low-rank latent vector c_KV (e.g., d_c=512), cache only the latent, and up-project at inference. Combined with RoPE-absorbing modifications, KV cache shrinks dramatically with negligible quality loss.

usecase_scenarios: Long-context serving where KV cache is the bottleneck

pros: Quality matches or beats GQA at same active params

Less ecosystem support than GQA (newer)
Up-projection adds compute at decode
metadata.implementation_guide: Implement: (1) down-project hidden state to c_KV = W_DKV(h) of shape [B,L,d_c]. Cache c_KV only. (2) For attention, up-project K = W_UK(c_KV), V = W_UV(c_KV). (3) For RoPE compatibility, split off a small separate latent c_KV' that gets RoPE-applied (since RoPE on the main latent would interfere with the up-projection math). DeepSeek-V3 further optimizes by absorbing W_UK into W_Q.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude does not use MLA (uses GQA), but MLA is a key innovation for production-grade long-context at low serving cost. Worth studying for any long-context-focused system.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
class MLA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_head, d_c=512, d_c_rope=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_c, self.d_c_rope = d_c, d_c_rope
        self.n_heads, self.d_head = n_heads, d_head
        self.W_DKV = nn.Linear(d_model, d_c, bias=False)
        self.W_UK = nn.Linear(d_c, n_heads*d_head, bias=False)
        self.W_UV = nn.Linear(d_c, n_heads*d_head, bias=False)
        self.W_Q = nn.Linear(d_model, n_heads*d_head, bias=False)
        # Plus: separate rope-aware latent branch omitted for brevity
    def forward(self, x):
        B,L,_ = x.shape
        c_kv = self.W_DKV(x)  # [B,L,d_c] -- CACHE THIS ONLY
        k = self.W_UK(c_kv).reshape(B,L,self.n_heads,self.d_head).transpose(1,2)
        v = self.W_UV(c_kv).reshape(B,L,self.n_heads,self.d_head).transpose(1,2)
        q = self.W_Q(x).reshape(B,L,self.n_heads,self.d_head).transpose(1,2)
        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True)

entries.eli5: When a sequence is too long for one GPU, split it across many GPUs in a ring - each GPU computes attention for its chunk, then passes its K/V to the next GPU, until everyone has seen all the context.
entries.purpose: Distribute long sequences across multiple GPUs (each holding a chunk), using ring communication to overlap attention compute with K/V block transfers, enabling training on sequences far longer than any single GPU can hold.
entries.input_dataset: Long sequences (100k-1M+ tokens) split into P chunks across P GPUs.
entries.outcome: Sequence length scales linearly with GPU count; near-perfect scaling up to thousands of GPUs.
benchmark_metrics: Sequence length per GPU (target: 32k+ per GPU, 1M+ total)
Loss curve parity with single-GPU attention

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L^2/P) compute per GPU; O(L/P * d) comm per ring step
pros: Sequence length is no longer bounded by single-GPU memory
Communication overlaps with compute (no idle GPUs)
cons: Requires high-bandwidth interconnect (InfiniBand/NVLink)
Load imbalance if attention is unevenly distributed
Higher latency for inference (ring traversal)
metadata.implementation_guide: Use Megatron-LM's context parallelism or implement with torch.distributed. Each GPU holds a chunk of the sequence. In the attention forward pass: (1) compute Q*K^T for local Q against local K, (2) send local K/V to next GPU and receive K/V from prev, (3) compute Q*K^T for local Q against received K, (4) repeat P-1 times. Use FlashAttention for each block computation. Overlap sends/receives with compute using CUDA streams.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's 200k context training almost certainly uses some form of context parallelism (Ring or Ulysses) since 200k tokens of activations cannot fit on a single GPU.
references: Liu et al. 2023 'Ring Attention with Blockwise Parallel Attention for Near-Infinite Context'

# Pseudocode - full Ring Attention is ~500 LOC
def ring_attn_forward(q, k, v, rank, world_size):
    # q: [B,H,L_local,d]  (local chunk on this GPU)
    outputs = []
    k_v_pairs = [(k, v)]
    reqs = []
    for step in range(world_size):
        # Async send k,v to next, recv from prev
        if step < world_size - 1:
            next_k = torch.empty_like(k); next_v = torch.empty_like(v)
            reqs = [
                dist.isend(k, dst=(rank+1)%world_size),
                dist.isend(v, dst=(rank+1)%world_size),
                dist.irecv(next_k, src=(rank-1)%world_size),
                dist.irecv(next_v, src=(rank-1)%world_size)]
        # Compute local block attention
        out_block = flash_attn_block(q, k, v)
        outputs.append(out_block)
        if step < world_size - 1:
            for r in reqs: r.wait()
            k, v = next_k, next_v
    return sum(outputs)

entries.purpose: Replace GELU/ReLU FFNs with a gated linear unit variant: FFN(x) = (Swish(xW1) ⊙ (xW3)) W2, improving quality at equal parameter count.

usecase_scenarios: Standard FFN in Llama, PaLM, Mistral, Gemma, Claude-style architectures
Quality upgrade drop-in replacing GELU FFNs

cons: Three matrices (extra memory bandwidth)
Requires careful hidden-dim rescaling to match parameter budgets

QK-norm variant to stabilize attention logits

cons: No mean-centering can matter in some non-LLM tasks
eps tuning matters at extreme quantization (FP8)

Then, replace it with Apex FusedRMSNorm or a custom Triton kernel. Fusing the variance calculation and the scaling into a single memory read/write pass is critical for training throughput.

entries.eli5: Instead of one giant brain, use many small expert brains; a traffic-controller decides which 1-2 experts handle each word, so the model gets huge capacity but only uses a fraction of it per word.
entries.purpose: Scale model capacity (parameters) sub-linearly in compute by activating only k of E expert FFNs per token via a learned router (top-k gating).
entries.input_dataset: Hidden states routed per token; balanced across experts during training.
usecase_scenarios: Large-capacity models at feasible training cost (Mixtral, Switch Transformer, Grok-1, DeepSeek-V2/V3)
entries.outcome: Higher quality-per-FLOP; sparse activation (e.g., 8 experts, top-2) keeps inference compute near a dense model ~1/4 the size.
benchmark_metrics: All-to-all communication overhead in expert parallelism

cons: Router collapse / load imbalance needs auxiliary losses
Large total memory footprint (all experts must be resident or offloaded)
Complex serving: token dropping, expert parallelism, uneven latency
metadata.implementation_guide: Implement a linear router that projects hidden states to num_experts dimensions, followed by a Softmax and Top-K selection. Crucially, you must add an auxiliary load-balancing loss (e.g., Switch Transformer loss) to the main training loss to prevent the router from collapsing and sending all tokens to just 1 or 2 experts. For production, use NVIDIA's Tutel library or Megatron-LM's optimized MoE layers to handle the complex all-to-all GPU communication.

usecase_scenarios: Self-speculative decoding without a separate draft model
Representation learning gains for small data regimes

Speculative acceptance rate from MTP heads

metadata.computational_complexity: +O(n * d^2) per token; ~negligible at GPU scale
pros: Cheap quality gains; elegant inference synergy
cons: Marginal gains on massive data; implementation complexity

Add their cross-entropy loss to the main final-layer loss with a small weight (e.g., 0.1). During inference, these heads can be used as the 'draft' model in speculative decoding, saving you from loading a separate draft model into memory.

entries.purpose: Linear-time sequence modeling via selective state-space models (Mamba-2, S6) with constant-memory recurrence; hybrids interleave SSM layers with full/sliding attention for quality + length scaling.

cons: Slight quality gap vs pure attention at small scale; in-context recall weaker
Kernel maturity and tooling behind FlashAttention ecosystem

For a hybrid architecture (which currently yields the best results), alternate between Mamba layers and standard Attention layers (e.g., 3 Mamba layers, 1 Attention layer). This retains the fast, linear-time throughput of Mamba while using the Attention layers to anchor in-context recall and precise data retrieval.

references: Gu & Dao 2023 'Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces'

entries.algorithm_name: DeepSeekMoE (Shared Experts + Fine-Grained Experts + Aux-Loss-Free Routing)
entries.eli5: A smarter MoE design: keep a few 'shared' experts always-on for general knowledge, plus many tiny specialized experts that the router picks from - and a clever trick to balance load without hurting the main loss.
entries.purpose: Improve MoE routing quality via (1) shared experts that handle universal knowledge, (2) fine-grained experts (smaller, more numerous) for specialization, (3) an auxiliary-loss-free load balancing scheme using bias adjustment.
entries.input_dataset: Standard pretraining tokens.
usecase_scenarios: When standard MoE suffers from router collapse or load imbalance
entries.outcome: Better quality than vanilla MoE at same FLOPs; near-perfect load balance without auxiliary loss interfering with main training.
benchmark_metrics: Quality vs vanilla MoE at equal active params

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L * (d_ff_shared * n_shared + d_ff_routed * top_k))
pros: Shared experts give universal knowledge 'for free'
cons: More implementation complexity than vanilla MoE
More expert modules to manage in distributed serving
metadata.implementation_guide: (1) Always-run shared experts: compute y_shared = sum(FFN_shared_i(x) for i in range(n_shared)). (2) Routed experts: small FFNs (e.g., 1/4 the size of dense FFN), with router selecting top_k. (3) Aux-loss-free balancing: maintain a per-expert bias term added to router logits; if an expert is over-utilized, increase its bias (decreasing its routing probability). This balancing happens outside the gradient path, so it does not interfere with the main loss.

entries.outcome: Stable convergence; beta2 around 0.95 for large batches, weight decay ~0.1 typical.
benchmark_metrics: Wall-clock steps/sec at fixed batch size

metadata.computational_complexity: O(P) memory for 2 optimizer states; ~3x parameter memory total (fp32 master + m + v)
pros: Extremely robust default; decades of tuning recipes
Well-understood interaction with LR schedules and warmup
cons: Optimizer state memory is huge at scale (motivates 8-bit optimizers)
Often beaten by Muon/Lion on matrix-parameter blocks at large scale
metadata.implementation_guide: Always use the FusedAdamW implementation provided by Apex or DeepSpeed to save massive amounts of memory bandwidth. Set betas=(0.9, 0.95) for large batch sizes. Keep your master weights in FP32, but compute gradients and updates in BF16. Apply weight decay only to 2D weight matrices (Linear layers), explicitly excluding LayerNorms, RMSNorms, and biases.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude pretraining uses AdamW (or a close variant like Muon for matrix params) with carefully tuned betas and weight decay. The exact recipe is proprietary.

entries.eli5: A new optimizer that beats AdamW on matrix parameters: it orthonormalizes the momentum using a 5-step Newton-Schulz iteration, so updates point in better directions. Used by Moonshot and others.
entries.purpose: Apply Newton-Schulz orthogonalization to the momentum buffer of 2D weight matrices (all Linear layers), giving better-conditioned updates and faster convergence than AdamW at equal compute.
entries.input_dataset: Model gradients (split into 2D matrix params and 1D vector params).
usecase_scenarios: Frontier-class pretraining where AdamW is the bottleneck
Hybrid: Muon for matrices, AdamW for embeddings/norms
entries.outcome: ~2x faster convergence vs AdamW on matrix params; better final loss at equal FLOPs.
benchmark_metrics: Final loss vs AdamW at equal steps

metadata.computational_complexity: +O(P * 5 * d^2) for Newton-Schulz on matrices; modest overhead
pros: Composes with AdamW for non-matrix params
cons: Newer (2024); less mature than AdamW
Newton-Schulz needs careful GPU kernel for speed
Hyperparameter interaction less explored
metadata.implementation_guide: Use a hybrid optimizer: Muon for all 2D Linear weight matrices, AdamW for embeddings, norms, biases, and the LM head. Muon update: (1) compute momentum m = 0.95*m + grad, (2) apply 5 Newton-Schulz iterations to orthogonalize m, (3) update w -= lr * m_orthogonal. Scale LR by sqrt(d_out/d_in) for shape-aware updates. Use the official Moonshot implementation for production.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Unknown if Claude uses Muon, but it's the leading open-source advance in optimizers for LLMs since 2024. Worth trying for any new pretraining run.
references: Jordan et al. 2024 'Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks'

entries.eli5: A family of optimizers that try to beat AdamW: Lion uses sign-only updates (smaller memory), Sophia uses a diagonal Hessian estimate for better long-range steps, SOAP does full-matrix preconditioning.
entries.purpose: Reduce optimizer state memory (Lion), improve conditioning (Sophia), or do full-matrix preconditioning (SOAP) - each targeting AdamW weaknesses for LLM-scale training.
entries.input_dataset: Model gradients.
usecase_scenarios: Sophia: long-horizon pretraining with better convergence
SOAP: best when matrix preconditioning adds acceptable overhead
entries.outcome: Lion: 2x smaller optimizer state. Sophia: 2x faster convergence on some LLM benchmarks. SOAP: best final loss on small/medium models but high overhead.

metadata.computational_complexity: Lion: O(P) less than AdamW. Sophia: +O(P) per Hessian estimate. SOAP: O(P * d^2) for preconditioning.
pros: Lion: smaller memory + often better final loss
cons: Lion: hyperparameter sensitive, sometimes unstable
Sophia: Hessian estimate adds noise
SOAP: heavy compute, doesn't scale to 100B+
metadata.implementation_guide: Lion: use lr = 1e-4 to 3e-4 (3-10x smaller than AdamW), betas=(0.9, 0.99). Update: m = b1*m + (1-b1)*grad; update = sign(b1*m + (1-b1)*grad); w -= lr * update; m_v = b2*m_v + (1-b2)*grad^2 (only for tracking, not used in update). Sophia: similar to Adam but uses Gaussian-Newton Hessian estimate as preconditioner. SOAP: use only for small models (<1B) - the preconditioning overhead is too high for frontier scale.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude most likely uses AdamW or Muon. Lion/Sophia/SOAP are research alternatives with mixed production adoption.
references: Chen et al. 2023 'Lion: Adapting Along Predecessors'
Liu et al. 2023 'Sophia: A Scalable Stochastic Second-order Optimizer'

entries.algorithm_name: Cosine LR Schedule with Warmup + Weight Decay Decoupling
entries.eli5: The learning rate starts tiny, ramps up gently so nothing explodes, then slowly cools down following a cosine curve to a minimum - like heating then slowly cooling an oven for the perfect bake.
entries.purpose: Schedule learning rate over training: linear or ramp warmup to peak, cosine decay to a floor, often with weight decay applied to matrices only (not norms/embeddings).
entries.input_dataset: Training step index and configured peak LR.
usecase_scenarios: Fine-tuning with short warmup and quick decay
entries.outcome: Well-behaved final loss; stable early training; reproducible decay-to-end behavior.
benchmark_metrics: Loss at LR floor vs constant-then-decay

metadata.computational_complexity: O(1) per step
pros: WSD variant allows flexible stopping and cooldown continuation
cons: Long-tail cosine wastes compute if early-stopped; WSD fixes this
Sensitive to warmup at very large batch sizes
metadata.implementation_guide: Implement a linear warmup for the first 1-2% of total training steps. After warmup, decay the learning rate following a cosine curve down to 10% of the peak learning rate. For continuous training or data-constrained regimes, look into WSD (Warmup-Stable-Decay) schedules which hold the LR constant for a long period before a final sharp decay.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses a long warmup (~2000 steps) followed by cosine decay. The exact peak LR and decay schedule are tuned per model size.
references: Loshchilov & Hutter 2017 'SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts'

entries.eli5: A smarter schedule that holds the LR steady in the middle for as long as you want, then does a short sharp decay at the end - lets you stop or extend training anytime without re-doing the schedule.
entries.purpose: Decouple stable-training phase from decay phase: warmup -> constant LR -> short (~10-20% of total) decay. Allows flexible stopping and compute-optimal reuse.
entries.input_dataset: Training step index.
usecase_scenarios: Continuous pretraining with uncertain total compute
Multiple model sizes from one training run (decimate at different points)
entries.outcome: Equivalent or better final loss vs cosine; ability to extend training without re-doing the schedule.
benchmark_metrics: Final loss at multiple stopping points

metadata.computational_complexity: O(1) per step
pros: Flexible stopping - any stable-phase checkpoint is usable
Multiple sizes from one run (stop decay early/late)
Better than cosine when total compute is uncertain
cons: Slightly worse than pure cosine if total compute is known in advance
Decay phase needs careful tuning (10-20% of total)
metadata.implementation_guide: Schedule: warmup 1-2% of total, stable for 80-90%, decay for 10-20%. During decay, use either linear or cosine from peak LR to 10% of peak. Save checkpoints at multiple points during decay to get a family of model sizes from one training run.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Modern Claude training likely uses WSD-style schedules for flexibility. The Anthropic team has emphasized reproducibility and continuation training as key engineering concerns.
references: Hu et al. 2024 'WSD: Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rate Schedule'

entries.eli5: Do most math in half-precision (fast, small), but keep a careful full-precision copy of weights and scale up tiny gradient values so they don't vanish - getting speed without losing accuracy.
entries.purpose: Accelerate training and reduce memory by computing in 16-bit (BF16 preferred: same exponent range as FP32) while maintaining FP32 master weights and loss scaling for FP16.
entries.input_dataset: Model weights, activations, gradients.
usecase_scenarios: Any GPU training (A100/H100 native BF16 tensor cores)
Activation checkpointing stacks where memory is critical
entries.outcome: ~2-3x throughput vs FP32, half the activation memory, with negligible quality impact (BF16 needs no loss scaling).
benchmark_metrics: Final loss parity vs FP32 baseline

metadata.computational_complexity: Same FLOPs but 2x+ tensor-core throughput vs FP32
cons: FP16 needs dynamic loss scaling; rare NaN bugs still occur
Some ops must stay FP32 (softmax accumulators, norms)
metadata.implementation_guide: Wrap your forward pass in torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16). BF16 is strongly preferred over FP16 for LLMs because its 8-bit exponent range matches FP32, completely eliminating the need for complex dynamic loss scaling and preventing NaN loss spikes. Keep your optimizer's master weight copies in FP32 to ensure precise weight updates.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude is trained in BF16 mixed precision with FP32 master weights. FP8 is now used in DeepSeek-V3 for further speedup.

entries.eli5: Instead of remembering every layer's output during the forward pass (huge memory), forget them and recompute each one on the fly during backprop - trading extra compute for massive memory savings.
entries.purpose: Store only inputs at selected layer boundaries; recompute intermediate activations during backward pass, enabling larger batches/models on limited memory.
entries.input_dataset: Transformer block activations.
usecase_scenarios: Long-sequence training where activations dominate memory
Selective checkpointing (recompute only attention, not MLP) in Megatron-LM
entries.outcome: ~30% more memory (activations) at cost of ~33% extra compute - enables larger effective batch or longer context.
benchmark_metrics: Max feasible batch size / context length

metadata.computational_complexity: One extra forward pass ~= 1.33x total training FLOPs for full checkpointing
pros: Dramatic memory savings (linear in depth instead of quadratic)
Selective variants (FlashAttention recomputes attention for free)
cons: ~25-33% throughput hit
RNG state management needed for dropout reproducibility
metadata.implementation_guide: Use torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint to wrap your Transformer blocks. For the optimal memory/compute tradeoff, use 'selective checkpointing': checkpoint only the Attention sub-layers (which have massive activation memory due to sequence length) but leave the FFN sub-layers un-checkpointed. This saves most of the memory while minimizing the 33% compute penalty.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's training uses selective activation checkpointing (recompute attention, keep FFN activations) to balance memory and throughput.
references: Chen et al. 2016 'Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost'

import torch.utils.checkpoint as ckpt
class Block(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        # Selective: checkpoint attention, NOT FFN
        x = x + ckpt.checkpoint(self.attn, self.norm1(x), use_reentrant=False)
        x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))  # FFN activations kept
        return x
# Or full: x = x + ckpt.checkpoint(self.attn, x); x = x + ckpt.checkpoint(self.ffn, x)

entries.eli5: Two safety rails: clip giant gradient spikes so they don't blow up training, and add a tiny RMSNorm to the Q and K vectors so attention scores never explode - together they prevent most loss spikes.
entries.purpose: Stabilize large-scale pretraining: (1) gradient clipping caps the global gradient norm to prevent explosion; (2) QK-norm applies RMSNorm to Q/K vectors before computing attention logits, preventing logit explosion at large widths.
entries.input_dataset: Gradients, Q/K activations.
usecase_scenarios: Training with large batch sizes (clip essential)
entries.outcome: Smoother loss curves; fewer divergent runs; ability to use higher LRs.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(P) for clip; O(L*d) for QK-norm
cons: Clipping can hide bugs (silently cap exploding gradients)
QK-norm adds a layer + params
metadata.implementation_guide: (1) After loss.backward() but before optimizer.step(), call torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0). (2) Add a small RMSNorm after Q and K projections (before RoPE) with no learned scale (or learned scale init to 1.0). This is QK-norm. It's essential for models >1B params.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses both gradient clipping (max_norm=1.0) and QK-norm for stable training at scale. These are non-negotiable for frontier-scale LLMs.
references: Pascanu et al. 2013 'On the difficulty of training Recurrent Neural Networks' (gradient clipping)

        self.q_norm = nn.RMSNorm(d//h, eps=1e-6)
        self.k_norm = nn.RMSNorm(d//h, eps=1e-6)
        # ... q,k,v projections
    def forward(self, x):
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        q = self.q_norm(q.reshape(..., self.h, self.d_h))
        k = self.k_norm(k.reshape(..., self.h, self.d_h))
        # ... attention

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

entries.algorithm_name: ZeRO / FSDP Distributed Data Parallel Sharding
entries.eli5: When training across many GPUs, instead of giving every GPU a full copy of the model, sharding splits the weights, gradients, and optimizer states across the fleet - together they hold one model, each GPU only a slice.
entries.purpose: Shard optimizer states (ZeRO-1), gradients (ZeRO-2), and parameters (ZeRO-3 / FSDP) across data-parallel ranks, gathering on demand during forward/backward.
entries.input_dataset: Model parameters, gradients, optimizer states across N GPUs.
usecase_scenarios: Multi-node fine-tuning where full copies don't fit
entries.outcome: Near-linear scaling; per-GPU memory reduced by up to Nx (ZeRO-3), enabling models far larger than one device.

metadata.computational_complexity: Compute unchanged; communication O(P * 2/N) per phase with overlap
pros: Enables trillion-parameter-scale training when combined with tensor/pipeline parallelism
cons: Communication overhead; needs careful overlap tuning
ZeRO-3 gathering can slow small-batch steps; complexity of nested wrapping
metadata.implementation_guide: Use PyTorch's native FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel). Wrap each individual Transformer block as a single FSDP unit. Enable backward_prefetch=BackwardPrefetch.BACKWARD_PRE and forward_prefetch=True to overlap communication with compute. Use ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD (equivalent to ZeRO-3) for maximum memory savings.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's training uses FSDP (or DeepSpeed ZeRO-3) combined with TP/PP for frontier-scale. The exact parallelism config is tuned per model size.
references: Rajbhandari et al. 2020 'ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models'

entries.eli5: Split the model three ways: cut it into horizontal slices across machines (pipeline), cut each layer's matrices into vertical strips (tensor), and duplicate data across the rest - so hundreds of GPUs train one monster model together.
entries.purpose: Combine tensor parallelism (intra-layer, NVLink-fast) and pipeline parallelism (inter-layer stages, point-to-point) with data parallelism to train models exceeding single-node memory/compute.
entries.input_dataset: Batches split into micro-batches flowing through pipeline stages.
usecase_scenarios: Interleaved schedules to reduce pipeline bubbles
Expert-parallel MoE combining all four dimensions
entries.outcome: Scales to thousands of GPUs; pipeline bubble fraction minimized via micro-batching and interleaving.

metadata.computational_complexity: Bubble overhead ~ (p-1)/m microbatches; tensor-parallel all-reduce per layer
pros: Only way to reach 10k+ GPU training runs
Tensor parallelism keeps activations on fastest interconnect
cons: Pipeline bubbles waste compute unless microbatch count >> stages
Extreme implementation complexity; debugging across 4 parallelism axes
metadata.implementation_guide: For models >70B, use Megatron-LM. Set Tensor Parallelism (TP) to the number of GPUs within a single node (e.g., 8) to utilize fast NVLink. Set Pipeline Parallelism (PP) across nodes. Use 'interleaved' pipeline schedules (e.g., 1F1B) to drastically reduce pipeline bubbles. Ensure you have 400Gbps+ InfiniBand between nodes for PP communication.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's training uses 3D (or 4D with expert) parallelism: TP within node, PP across nodes, DP across replicas. The exact config is tuned per model size.
references: Narayanan et al. 2021 'Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters'

entries.eli5: Experiments revealed a precise power-law recipe: for a fixed compute budget, model size and training data should grow together - most big models were undertrained, and smaller models fed more data are smarter per FLOP.
entries.purpose: Determine compute-optimal model size N and token count D for budget C ~= 6ND via power-law loss L(N,D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta (alpha~=0.34, beta~=0.28).
entries.input_dataset: Many small training runs sweeping (N, D) to fit scaling exponents.
usecase_scenarios: Deciding model size vs. training length for a GPU budget
Predicting large-run loss from small-run extrapolation
Data-constrained regimes: repetition, curriculum, and dedup valuation
entries.outcome: Compute-optimal ratio ~20 tokens per parameter (Chinchilla); guides Llama-style overtraining for inference efficiency.
benchmark_metrics: Extrapolation error of fitted scaling law

metadata.computational_complexity: Fitting is O(#runs); inference of optimal point is closed-form
pros: Predictive budgeting: avoids massively undertrained models
Principled trade-off between training and inference cost
cons: Laws shift with architecture (MoE, multimodal), data quality, and curriculum
Extrapolation beyond fitted range is risky (emergent capabilities)
metadata.implementation_guide: Before committing to a massive training run, train a series of small proxy models (e.g., 100M to 1B params) on varying amounts of data. Fit the Chinchilla scaling curves to your specific data quality and architecture. The golden rule is ~20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training, but if you are constrained by data, overtrain a smaller model (Llama-3 style) for better inference efficiency.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Anthropic uses scaling law fits to decide Claude model sizes. The exact exponents for their architecture and data are proprietary, but they follow Chinchilla-style compute-optimal reasoning.
references: Hoffmann et al. 2022 'Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models' (Chinchilla)
Kaplan et al. 2020 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models'
Muennighoff et al. 2023 'Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models'

Ds = np.array([2e9, 6e9, 2e10, 6e10])
Ls = np.array([3.5, 3.0, 2.7, 2.4])  # measured val losses

entries.eli5: When training on huge contexts (100k+ tokens), split the sequence itself across GPUs - each GPU processes a chunk, and they coordinate via ring or all-to-all to compute attention across the whole sequence.
entries.purpose: Distribute long-sequence activations (not just weights) across GPUs by partitioning the sequence dimension, enabling training on contexts far longer than any single GPU can hold.
entries.input_dataset: Long sequences (16k-1M+ tokens).
usecase_scenarios: Long-CoT training for reasoning models (o1, R1)
entries.outcome: Sequence length scales linearly with context-parallel size; near-perfect scaling up to 64+ GPUs per sequence.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L^2 / cp_size) compute per GPU; O(L / cp_size * d) communication per step
pros: Sequence length no longer bounded by single GPU memory
cons: Requires high-bandwidth interconnect
Adds a 4th parallelism axis (complexity)
Ulysses needs all-to-all (more comm than ring)

(2) For attention, either ring-pass K/V (Megatron CP/Ring Attention) or use all-to-all to repartition Q/K/V by head dim (Ulysses). (3) Overlap communication with compute via CUDA streams. Combine with TP within a node and DP/PP across nodes.

entries.purpose: Reduce activation memory in tensor-parallel regions by partitioning the sequence dimension for norms/embeddings/FFN, then all-to-all convert to head-parallel for attention, enabling longer sequences at fixed TP size.

usecase_scenarios: Reducing activation memory in TP regions of Megatron-LM

pros: Halves activation memory in TP region
Ulysses: better than Ring Attention for moderate P
cons: All-to-all is more expensive than all-reduce (latency-sensitive)
Adds comm overhead per layer

Before attention, do an all-to-all to convert from [sp_size, L/sp, d] to [sp_size, L, d/sp] (head-parallel). After attention, all-to-all back. references: Korthikanti et al. 2022 'Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models'

entries.eli5: In MoE training, put different experts on different GPUs - tokens get routed to the right GPU, computed, and sent back. This is the 4th dimension of parallelism, layered on top of TP/PP/DP.
entries.purpose: Distribute MoE experts across GPUs (each GPU holds a subset of experts), using all-to-all to send tokens to the right expert's GPU and back. The 4th parallelism axis for MoE training.
entries.input_dataset: Token hidden states + router decisions.
usecase_scenarios: Combining with TP/PP/DP for 4D MoE parallelism
entries.outcome: Trillion-parameter MoE training (DeepSeek-V3: 671B); each GPU holds only a slice of experts.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(L * top_k * d_ff) compute; O(L * top_k * d) all-to-all comm
pros: Only way to fit 100B+ MoE models
Scales linearly with EP size for fixed expert count
cons: All-to-all is the bottleneck (latency-sensitive)
Token dropping on capacity overflow
Load imbalance across expert GPUs
metadata.implementation_guide: Set EP size such that each GPU holds 1-2 experts (e.g., 64 experts across 64 GPUs). Use all-to-all to dispatch tokens to their assigned expert's GPU, compute the FFN, then all-to-all to gather results back. Use a capacity_factor of 1.25-1.5 to allow some buffer for unbalanced routing. Token-drop on overflow, or use Expert Choice routing for better balance.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: If Claude uses MoE, expert parallelism is essential. The exact EP/TP/PP/DP config is proprietary.
references: Lepikhin et al. 2020 'GShard: Scaling Giant Models using Conditional Computation'

import torch.distributed as dist
def moe_ep_forward(x, router, experts, ep_group):
    # x: [B, L, d]; router picks expert per token
    route_idx = router(x).argmax(-1)
    # All-to-all: dispatch tokens to expert GPUs
    # Each GPU only computes its local experts
    local_tokens = all_to_all_dispatch(x, route_idx, ep_group)
    local_out = experts[0](local_tokens)  # this GPU's expert
    # All-to-all back: gather to original ordering
    return all_to_all_gather(local_out, route_idx, ep_group)

entries.algorithm_name: Fault Tolerance & Async Checkpointing for Long Runs
entries.eli5: When you train on 10,000 GPUs for weeks, hardware failures are guaranteed - save your progress constantly (in the background) and recover automatically when a GPU dies, so a single failure doesn't lose weeks of work.
entries.purpose: Survive GPU/network failures during multi-week training runs via (1) async background checkpointing to avoid stalling training, (2) automatic failure detection and recovery, (3) resumable optimizer state.
entries.input_dataset: Training state (model, optimizer, scheduler, data loader position).
usecase_scenarios: Any pretraining run >1 day on >64 GPUs
entries.outcome: Recovery from any single-node failure in <10 minutes; near-zero training progress lost.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(P) save in background thread; O(P) load on recovery
pros: Essential for any large run (MTBF on 10k GPUs is hours)
Distributed format (DCP) scales to TB checkpoints
cons: Engineering complexity (state serialization, RNG, dataloader position)
Async uploads can fill disk if network is slow
Checkpoint version compatibility across code versions
metadata.implementation_guide: Use torch.distributed.checkpoint (DCP) for distributed save (each GPU writes only its shards in parallel). Save every 1000-5000 steps. Use a background thread to upload to S3/GCS while training continues. For recovery: detect failure via heartbeat, restart job from latest checkpoint, restore model+optimizer+scheduler+RNG+dataloader state. Save RNG state explicitly for reproducibility.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Anthropic has emphasized reliability of Claude training as a key engineering feat. Their checkpointing and recovery system handles 10k+ GPU runs with high uptime.
metadata.code_snippet:
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
state_dict = {'model': model.state_dict(),
              'optim': optim.state_dict(),
              'step': step, 'rng': torch.get_rng_state()}
# Async save (returns future)
future = dcp.async_save(state_dict, storage_writer=s3_writer)
# On recovery:
loaded = dcp.load(state_dict, storage_reader=s3_reader)

entries.eli5: After the model learns language by reading everything, teach it manners and job skills by showing it thousands of examples of ideal conversations and tasks, so it learns to follow instructions instead of just continuing text.
entries.purpose: Adapt a base model to follow instructions, answer questions, and behave helpfully via maximum-likelihood training on curated (prompt, response) demonstrations.
entries.input_dataset: Instruction datasets: Alpaca, OpenAssistant, LIMA, Tulu, UltraChat - tens of thousands to millions of examples.
usecase_scenarios: First stage of all chat models (Llama-2-Chat, Mistral-Instruct, Claude)
Behavioral cloning of a target persona/format
entries.outcome: A model that follows instructions in the demonstrated style; quality strongly dependent on data curation over quantity (LIMA: 1k examples suffice).
benchmark_metrics: Catastrophic forgetting of pretrain knowledge (measured by base benchmarks)

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N_sft * tokens * 6 * params) FLOPs; tiny vs pretraining
pros: Data quality >> quantity; format teaches behavior
cons: Can cause knowledge forgetting and over-fitting to verbose styles
Doesn't directly optimize for preferences - needs RLHF/DPO next
Highly sensitive to noisy/prompt-injected demonstration data

entries.eli5: A twin of the chatbot that doesn't write - it judges. Trained on thousands of 'answer A vs answer B, which is better?' votes, it outputs a scalar score that RLHF then pushes upward.
entries.purpose: Model human preferences P(y_w preferred over y_l | x) = sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)) with a scalar head; typically initialized from the SFT model with a value head.
entries.input_dataset: Human (or AI) pairwise preference comparisons over prompt-response pairs.
usecase_scenarios: Iterative online preference collection (fresh pairs against latest policy)
entries.outcome: A scalar reward function aligned with labeler preferences; accuracy 65-75% typical on held-out pairs.
benchmark_metrics: Robustness to reward hacking (length bias detection)

key_hyperparameters: RM size (typically same as policy or smaller)
reward head pooling (last token vs mean)
metadata.computational_complexity: Training ~= SFT cost on pair data; inference = one forward + scalar head
pros: Directly encodes labeler preferences; enables both PPO and BoN/DPO pipelines
cons: Single RM is hackable (length bias, sycophancy cues); ensembling and regularization needed
Preference labels are noisy and expensive
metadata.implementation_guide: Initialize the RM from your SFT checkpoint. Remove the final LM Head and replace it with a single linear layer outputting a scalar. Train using the Bradley-Terry loss on your (chosen, rejected) pairs. To prevent the RM from simply rewarding longer, more verbose answers, add a small length penalty to the reward score or train on length-controlled preference data.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude uses a sophisticated reward modeling stack, possibly including ensemble RMs and multi-objective rewards (helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty). Constitutional AI principles are encoded into the preference data generation.

entries.algorithm_name: RLHF via PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization with Reward Model)
entries.eli5: Have humans rank pairs of answers to train a 'taste judge' neural network, then use reinforcement learning to push the chatbot's answers up the judge's score - while a leash (KL penalty) keeps it from drifting into weird gibberish.
entries.purpose: Optimize a language model policy pi against a learned reward model r(x,y) using PPO with KL regularization to a reference model, maximizing E[r] - beta*KL(pi || pi_ref).
entries.input_dataset: Prompts + human preference rankings (chosen vs rejected pairs) -> trained Bradley-Terry reward model.
usecase_scenarios: The original recipe behind ChatGPT, Claude, Llama-2-Chat
Style control (verbosity, formatting, persona) beyond SFT
entries.outcome: Significant preference win rates (AlpacaEval/Chatbot Arena) over SFT-only models; tunable beta controls conservativeness.
benchmark_metrics: KL divergence vs reference at convergence
Arena Elo / AlpacaEval LC win rate

metadata.computational_complexity: Rollout generation dominates: ~4x SFT cost per step (policy + ref + reward + value forwards)
pros: Directly optimizes human preferences; large measurable gains
Reward model reusable across iterations (online RLHF)
cons: Extremely complex, unstable, expensive pipeline (4 models in memory)
Reward hacking/over-optimization (length bias, sycophancy)
Needs constant fresh human preference data
metadata.implementation_guide: Use OpenRLHF or TRL. This requires 4 models in memory simultaneously: Policy, Reference, Reward, and Value (Critic). Use DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 to shard them. Keep the KL penalty coefficient (beta) small (0.01 to 0.05) to prevent the policy from collapsing or diverging too far from the reference model. Monitor the reward score closely; if it spikes while actual human quality drops, you are experiencing reward hacking.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude 1 and 2 used PPO RLHF extensively. Claude 3+ has moved toward more efficient alternatives (DPO, Constitutional AI), but PPO remains a reference for understanding alignment.
references: Schulman et al. 2017 'Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms'

entries.algorithm_name: DPO / IPO / KTO (Direct Preference Optimization family)
entries.eli5: Skip the reward model and the reinforcement learning entirely - train directly on pairs of good vs bad answers with a clever loss that secretly encodes the same RLHF math, making preference training as simple as fine-tuning.
entries.purpose: Derive the RLHF objective's closed-form optimum to train the policy directly on preference pairs: maximize log-sigmoid of beta*(log pi(y_w|x) - log pi_ref(y_w|x) - same for y_l).
entries.input_dataset: Preference pairs (prompt, chosen, rejected) - same data as RLHF.
usecase_scenarios: Cheap alignment for open models (Zephyr, Tulu-2, Llama-3-Instruct recipes)
Iterative DPO / online DPO with fresh model generations
Style/format alignment without reward model maintenance
entries.outcome: Arena-level quality close to PPO at a fraction of pipeline complexity and compute.
benchmark_metrics: Implicit reward accuracy on held-out pairs

metadata.computational_complexity: ~2x SFT cost (policy + reference forward); no rollouts, no reward/value models
pros: Simple, stable, cheap; single stage on static pairs
Closed-form derivation; many robust variants (IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO)
cons: Static data can't adapt like online RL; tends to lengthen responses
Slightly below best online RLHF at very large compute budgets
Sensitive to beta and pair quality (noisy labels hurt directly)
metadata.implementation_guide: Use the TRL DPOTrainer. Load your SFT model as the 'policy' and keep a frozen, detached copy as the 'reference' model. To save VRAM, apply LoRA to the policy model. Set beta=0.1 and a very low learning rate (5e-6). DPO is essentially a logistic regression on the log-probabilities of the chosen vs rejected responses. It is vastly more stable than PPO and should be your default alignment choice.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude 3+ reportedly uses DPO-style alignment (or its variants) for efficiency. Constitutional AI pairs naturally feed into DPO training.
references: Rafailov et al. 2023 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model'
Ethayarajh et al. 2024 'KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization'

entries.algorithm_name: Constitutional AI / RLAIF (Critique-Revision with AI Feedback)
entries.eli5: Instead of paying humans to rate every answer, give the model a written 'constitution' of principles, have it critique and rewrite its own harmful answers against those principles, then train on those revisions - scaling alignment without scaling human labeling.
entries.purpose: Replace human preference labels with AI-generated feedback: self-critique -> revision against explicit principles -> SL-CAI (SFT on revisions) and RL-CAI (RLAIF with AI preference model).
entries.input_dataset: Constitution (list of principles), prompts, model's own harmful/edge-case responses.
usecase_scenarios: The alignment approach behind Claude (Constitutional AI paper)
Harmlessness training at scale with minimal human labels
Principle-based behavior shaping (refusal style, transparency norms)
entries.outcome: Models that critique themselves against written principles; harmlessness from AI feedback comparable to human feedback, with different failure modes.
benchmark_metrics: Over-refusal rate trade-off (strong rejections on benign prompts)

metadata.computational_complexity: N_critique x inference cost for revisions + standard RLHF/DPO training on outputs
pros: Scales alignment oversight without proportional human labeling
Interpretable, editable behavior specification (the constitution text)
cons: Constitution is hand-written - encoding human values lossily
Can produce systematic over-refusals; principle conflicts need arbitration
Feedback model inherits and can amplify its own biases
metadata.implementation_guide: Phase 1 (SLAIF): Write a 'Constitution' of 10-20 explicit principles. Prompt the model to generate responses to adversarial/harmful prompts. Have the model critique its own response based on the Constitution, then rewrite it. SFT the model on these revised, safe responses. Phase 2 (RLAIF): Generate pairs of responses, have the AI judge which is better based on the Constitution to create a synthetic preference dataset, then run DPO on it.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Constitutional AI is THE signature alignment method of Claude. The constitution includes principles from sources like the UN Declaration of Human Rights, Anthropic's research on helpfulness, and operational principles for non-deception. The exact constitution text has been partially published.
references: Bai et al. 2022 'Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback' (Anthropic)
Lee et al. 2023 'RLAIF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback'

entries.algorithm_name: RLAIF Best-of-N Distillation & Reward Model Ensembles
entries.eli5: Let a panel of AI judges (an ensemble of reward models) score many candidate answers and keep the best - then distill that selection ability into the model itself so it doesn't need the panel at inference time.
entries.purpose: Use AI feedback to select/reject samples (rejection sampling fine-tuning, RFT) and train reward ensembles that are more robust than single RM to hacking.
entries.input_dataset: Prompts + N sampled responses + AI judge scores.
usecase_scenarios: Multi-objective alignment: helpfulness, harmlessness, verbosity RM ensemble with weighted votes
entries.outcome: Distilled best-of-N behavior; ensemble reward curves that are harder to over-optimize/hack.

metadata.computational_complexity: Training-free at inference (BoN) or distillation cost ~= SFT on winners
pros: Training-free quality boost (BoN); scalable via distillation
cons: BoN at inference is expensive (N forwards) and doesn't compose with low latency
RM ensembles can still share blind spots
metadata.implementation_guide: For Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT): Generate N=16 responses per prompt using the SFT model. Score them using an ensemble of 3-5 Reward Models. SFT the model exclusively on the highest-scoring responses. This is highly effective for math and coding, and is a core part of the Llama-3 and DeepSeek-Math recipes.
metadata.claude_specific_notes: Claude's alignment uses RLAIF extensively for harmlessness training, with Constitutional AI principles driving the AI judge. Ensemble rewards reduce single-RM hacking vulnerabilities.
references: Dong et al. 2023 'RAFT: Reward rAnked FineTuning for Generative Foundation Model Alignment'
